subsubtopic: LIBERAL LEADERSHIP CANDIDATE'S STATEMENT ON REDUCING DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two position-three position John Turner, who is running for the leadership of the Grits, has stated that he is going to reduce the deficit by $ 15 billion, but he is having difficulty explaining how he plans to do this.
As a suggestion, if Mr. Turner could provide us with the formula he used when he was Finance Minister to create a deficit of $5 billion from a surplus of $700 million in a matter of three years, as well as how he managed to increase spending by 99.8 per cent and raise the cost of living 38.5 per cent, we could perhaps be on to the formula needed to reverse Grit uncontrolled spending.
Obviously the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has been unable to curtail this uncontrolled spending trend as government spending on a public accounts basis has increased a whopping 668 per cent. If Mr. Turner would only be so kind as to provide us with the formula, following the next election the Progressive Conservative Government could use the formula in reverse to end the sinking of this country into further debt.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF UNEMPLOYED WORKERS OVER 50 YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is frustrating to be over 50 years of age for both men and women, when they are looking for work. They work the best years of their lives in an industry. As soon as things get tough and the demand for the product slackens, the first to be laid off are those over 50. To make matters worse, no other firm, or the federal Government, is interested in hiring women or men over 50.
The Government and some businesses say: "You cannot work long enough to build up a pension", or: "Sorry, we don't have any openings", and then confide that they want younger people. As a result of bankruptcies of businesses and firms closing their doors, they are made to feel unwanted.
"I have worked like a horse all my life", a man 56 years of age said to me, "and now I am treated like a dog." He is becoming bitter, and I do not blame him. He and thousands like him are not responsible for the recession. They hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) tell the House, day after day, about the millions of dollars that they are providing for the unemployed, and when they go to the employment offices, or to government offices, they are brushed off and told: "The course is full; come back in three months", or: "You are too old to learn a new trade; go on welfare."
I ask this Government when some of these millions it talks about are going to eke their way down to the level of the unemployed. When? I wish the Government would realize what these people who have worked all their lives are now going through. Reduced federal taxes and the elimination of red tape would be of some help. Then Canadians would invest their money and provide work in Canada instead of exporting our money and jobs.

subsubtopic: ATTITUDE OF QUEBEC GOVERNMENT-REQUEST THAT FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, early this week I was on the lower North Shore where I met with fishermen from Blanc-Sablon and Kegaska, to find a way to settle the dispute between Mr. Garon and the fishermen about the installation of certain facilities on the middle and lower North Shore.
Mr. Speaker, considering the fact that Quebec is scarcely prepared to move on this issue, I would ask the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) to see to it that salting sheds and ice machines are installed on federal property, and to spend the $10 million where we can spend it at this time, in order to help these fishermen, who could be operational very soon.
Where the Province refuses to co-operate in various fishing villages, it will have only itself to blame for the consequences. At the present time, Mr. Garon is acting against the interests of fishermen on the middle and lower North Shore, and I feel, Mr. Speaker, that we must speak out against this behaviour.

May 4, 1984
The people, including the fishermen, are now being held hostage by the Province of Quebec.
The federal Government is still prepared to maintain the funding of $10 million for the middle and lower North Shore, but if we do not succeed in reaching an agreement with the Province of Quebec we will only be able to install the facilities in question where the federal Government owns the land.
Mr. Speaker, my point is that the money is still available, but if we cannot help fishermen where the land does not belong to the federal Government, Mr. Garon will have only himself and his government to blame.

subsubtopic: RIDING MOUNTAIN NATIONAL PARK-CALL FOR PUBLIC CONSULTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak under Standing Order 21 regarding Riding Mountain National Park, the only national park in Manitoba. The Minister responsible for national parks is currently conducting a review of the Department's plans, and is upgrading its 1977 master plan into a management plan. The recent departmental newsletter indicated that there will be consultations in Step 2 and Step 5 of the revision process.
We have some real concern about the lack of public consultations in the past. This kind of public review is something which only happens once every five years or so, and we call upon the Minister to provide an opportunity for genuine consultation this time around.
My own office has a list of some 20 items of concern. For example, Grandview Council met with me again last week and made representations about having the Grandview-Rossbum Road opened up through the park. Church group licences within the park expire in 1985. It is important that these groups that work well with young people be included in the new management plan. The Dauphin Town Council has expressed real concern about the stability of the town's water supply. I could go on.
It is important that the Minister personally hear the concerns of the municipalities, of the residents of the area, and of concerned organizations. I have approached the Minister about coming to meet with the area municipalities and I am pleased that he has given agreement in principle to that proposal. I now urge him to come quickly to some decision on the date when he will be available.

Mr. Speaker, the incompetence of the Government manifests itself no more profoundly than in the area of housing. The Government has failed to meet even the most reasonable expectations of Canadians in terms of government programs designed to provide affordable shelter.
The Government has failed completely to develop a social housing program. In fact it has become increasingly difficult, if not impossible, for even the average Canadian with a steady income to find shelter. The high cost of money, fluctuating interest rates, and the current increases in interest rates create new fears and anxieties for Canadians who are worrying about what to do when their mortgages come due.
What are the options, Sir? In 1979 we provided the option of mortgage deductibility programs. It is always interesting to hear members of the NDP berating the Government for failing to respond to a crisis in our country since they supported the Government and made sure that such an innovative program, which would have saved thousands of people from losing their homes, was not implemented.
There are other programs which are available. The Governments of other countries do much better. They look at housing as a social right and, in so doing, make sure that the subsidies or innovative programs that they implement are not designed to help the banks or mortgage companies but are designed to help average home owners.

Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 21 because of the Government's misrepresentation of its intention last June 29 when it passed Bill C-95, an Act to provide for government-operated pool systems on combinations of athletic contests and events, and to amend the Criminal Code and the Income Tax Act.
In statements and replies in the House and in committee, the Government took pains to ensure that the legislation would not enable the Government to engage in a lottery. On that basis, and because of the clearly indicated importance of this legislation for the funding of the 1988 Olympic Games in Calgary, the House passed that legislation. What has been created on the basis of that legislation is not what was understood as having been within the powers of that legislation.
On December 7, 1982, before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, the then responsible Minister said in reference to the 1979 agreement with the provinces:
We have chosen to respect that, and if we establish this sports pool we will continue to respect the agreement we have with the provinces and we will expect them to continue to do so also... because the agreement we have with the
May 4, 1984

provinces deals with the lottery field. Our legal opinion is that a sports pool is something very different.
The fact that the Government has chosen to change, by Order in Council, and in the dead of night, the sports pool legislation passed after lengthy debate in the House, underlines the urgent need for a full and public airing of this matter.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR REVITALIZATION OF WEST COAST INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Cassiar Packing Company went into receivership last summer, hundreds of shoreworkers, fishermen, and small businesses had their livelihood severely disrupted, if not completely eliminated. The banks, the few remaining conglomerates, and the Department of Fisheries have squeezed this industry dry and it is now time to turn the tide and bring vitality and employment back to the West Coast fishing industry.
The Minister of Fisheries has stated to me that his Department, in conjunction with the Department of Indian Affairs and the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, is presently working on a proposal. It is a proposal to get the Cassiar fishing fleet back onto the grounds, to renew the gainful employment Cassiar shoreworkers once experienced, and to rejuvenate the financial future of the small businesses and the community services which depend on Cassiar producing at full steam.
I believe it is incumbent upon the Minister to reveal publicly his Government's intention to see the Cassiar operation in Prince Rupert and the Skeena slough open for the summer season. Too little has been done to date. For this operation to start up, details must be finalized and made public by the end of this month. My constituents want jobs, not welfare. The Government should not forget that over $600 million has gone to restructure the Quebec and East Coast fishing industries. How about a sense of fairness?

speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance may have full confidence in the Governor of the Bank of Canada, but clearly his own cabinet colleagues do not have confidence in the Minister of Finance and his monetary policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. My question exemplifies the sense of frustration and injustice felt in Newfoundland today over the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada to declare the Churchill Falls Water Rights Reversion Act to be ultra vires. Since the Churchill Falls power contract represents probably the greatest grievance in this country today and is a festering sore in Confederation, what steps does the Government of Canada intend to take to correct this great injustice to the people of Newfoundland?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Premier of Newfoundland plays a very hard game. Sometimes he goes the political road, and at other times the legal road, and most of the time both roads. When he loses, he blames the federal Government.
Be that as it may, the decision of the court was on constitutional grounds. My hon. friend knows that this is a provincial matter. His colleague from St. John's West was suggesting a mediation role by the Prime Minister. That is about all that can be done by the federal Government, unless the federal Government wants to be chastised by the Supreme Court for acting in an area which is not of its jurisdiction.
Mediation is not a bad idea, and I understand that in the past, Ministers of Energy, Mines and Resources have made suggestions that there could be a mediation, a conciliation, or even an arbitration for that matter. However, that necessitates the consent of the two parties.
For the time being I think we should let some days pass. I observed that the Premier and the Minister of Energy of Quebec immediately offered resumption of previous negotiations which apparently had made some progress. I read in the paper this morning that the Premier of Newfoundland was still hoping that there could be a negotiated solution to this matter.

I would say to the Minister that the Government of Canada clearly has a responsibility here, given the fact that there is a separatist Government in Quebec and that it buys the power from Newfoundland for less than three mills and sells it to the Americans for 28 mills. That is $800 million for Quebec and $8 million for Newfoundland.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while the National Energy Board has the authority to regulate the construction of new interprovincial power lines, it does not have the authority to regulate interprovincial electricity exchanges. That is an area where the federal Government can act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really do not know the technical answer to that, if such an amendment were considered. Nevertheless, the gist of what I said still stands, namely that this is provincial jurisdiction. It is a dispute between two provincial Governments.
The Supreme Court decision made the implication that it was on constitutional grounds, not on social or economic grounds. I think many people will agree that there is an element of imbalance in the original contract, and I would think that the provincial Government of Quebec does agree to that, to a certain extent. That is my reading of the press on that subject.
Negotiations took place before. I read in the press that there was agreement that they were progressing. It seems to me that the provincial Government of Quebec is not obstinate on the subject. I think it is willing to compromise and willing to discuss the matter. It seems to me that, now that there is a certainty on the legal side, the provincial Governments of Newfoundland and Quebec should get together to negotiate a fair settlement.

Member's own province, have opted out of this program which by law requires 25 per cent participation of provincial Governments.

May 4, 1984

The Hon. Member for Edmonton North has given the Chair the usual notice of his intention to move the adjournment of the House pursuant to Standing Order 30. The issues related to the Act to provide for government operated pool systems on combinations of athletic contests and events have quite obviously been a continuing concern for many Members of the House, but the Chair has reservations as to the urgency for debate and as to whether it is a proper subject to be debated under Standing Order 30.
The principle involved in this case is that a review of an existing law can only, under the rarest of circumstances, be regarded as an emergency provision under Standing Order 30.
On April 30, 1975 Speaker Jerome defined this principle when he said:
-that the emergency provisions pursuant to Standing Order 26 ought to be distinguished, or their use ought to be distinguished from those items which, in a regular legislative program of the House of Commons and regular legislative consideration, can come before the House by way of amendments to existing statutes, or in any case will come before it in other ways.
My predecessor, Madam Sauve, also ruled in the same way on similar applications on July 9, 1980 and on July 15, 1980.
It is clear to the Chair, therefore, that this subject does not meet the strict emergency provision of the Standing Order. Furthermore, the Hon. Member has other avenues for debate open to him. Next Thursday has been designated as an allotted day and the estimates for the current fiscal year are presently before the committees of the House.
For these, reasons, I must decline the Hon. Member's request.

The House resumed from Tuesday, May 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet (for Mr. Gray) that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-24. It is called an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act, but the burden of my argument will be that it should be more accurately called a Bill to erode further Parliament's existing very modest control over 183 federal Crown corporations and subsidiaries.
Why do I say that? First, I point out that the Bill has 134 pages. I put it to you, Sir, that if the Customs Act, which we were discussing a few days ago, was difficult for anyone to read, including lawyers, this one is even more so.
The Bill, as drafted, is basically enabling legislation. It gives wide regulation-making powers rather than specifying clearly and in detail how the mechanism of control, direction and accountability are going to work. Without seeing those regulations-I point out that the Government has provided no regulations to date nor given any indication it is prepared to do so-it is impossible to know precisely what the Government intends with this Bill. For example, C-I and C-II corporations are required to submit corporate plans, but the form and content of those plans is left to regulations and not specified. Operating in capital budgets are required from C-I and C-II corporations, but the Bill authorizes the Treasury Board, by regulation, to exempt any corporation or group of corporations from the requirement. In the Government's quest for flexibility, and due to the haste with which the Bill was prepared, the legislation represents a regime of excessive administrative discretion.
Second, on the vital question of ministerial responsibility, I cannot in passing help but note that earlier, Sir, the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) made the comment about firing the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Pepin) told us, in effect, that that was not a question of ministerial responsibility, that it was done during a commercial break. So I ask what concept of ministerial
responsibility do Hon. Members opposite accept? Bill C-24 leaves the Minister as the de jure shareholder, but requires Cabinet to approve most major initiatives such as the appointment of directors, auditors, chairman and chief executive officers and the approval of operating and capital budgets, corporate plans and by-laws. In short, Bill C-24 continues the current situation where the Minister is nominally responsible but Cabinet exercises the burden of the shareholders' powers. In being accountable to many, Crown corporations will, in my view, continue to be responsible to no one.
Third, again on the important question of boards of directors, the Bill, as you will know, Mr. Speaker, proposes that the duties and responsibilities of directors under the Canada Business Corporations Act apply mutatis mutandis-if I may be forgiven a bit of Latin-to directors of Crown corporations. Bill C-24 goes into no detail on how the duties or responsibilities would apply in specific instances. And is that not the important matter in terms of practical experience?
More importantly, Bill C-24 seriously erodes the practical powers and prerogatives of directors and undermines the attempt to upgrade their duties and responsibilities. In the private sector, the essential prerogative of a board is to monitor the chief executive officer's stewardship of the corporation, to hire or fire him and set his or her remuneration. Under Bill C-24 all these functions are exercised by Cabinet. Cabinet appoints the chairman and chief executive officer and sets their remuneration, appoints the auditor, approves, varies or rescinds by-laws, and may direct a board to approve a by-law. In addition, the chief executive officer, who is generally not the chairman of the board, is required to advise the Government of any significant variations in actual performance from approved corporate plans, budgets and the like, giving the reasons.
Fourth, again on the important question of the proliferation of new Crown corporations, on the surface Bill C-24 takes some positive steps to avert the unnecessary proliferation of Crown corporations. It appears that in future the creation of a Crown corporation will require parliamentary approval via a special Act. There are major loopholes, however, and I will list four of them. First, the parliamentary approval process applies only to parent corporations, not to subsidiaries. It has been through subsidiaries, you will know, Mr. Speaker, that the greatest proliferation has occurred.
Second, the juxtaposition of Section 100 with Section 155 appears to turn the prohibition on its head by allowing parent corporations to be set up under the CBCA with only Cabinet approval and a motion in Parliament.
Third, the Government will still be able to incorporate parent Crown corporations where an existing Act of Parliament allows it to do so. As you will know, Mr. Speaker, there are a sufficient number of such Acts now in existence to satisfy most of the need for new Crown corporations.
Fourth, Bill C-24 could be interpreted, I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, to suggest that Ministers, as representatives of the
May 4, 1984

Crown, many not be bound by Bill C-24's prohibition on the creation of parent corporations.
More generally with respect to the question of proliferation, the restrictions placed on debate of any special Act, which, as you know, Mr. Speaker, is 30 days in committee and seven hours of continuous debate in the House, are too severe, in my opinion. Placing any such restrictions is, in any event, contrary to a fundamental principle that one Parliament does not bind, by legislation, the internal workings of a future Parliament.
Hear, hear!

The Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) is very perceptive, Mr. Speaker. In this respect, therefore, Bill C-24 represents a significant and dangerous precedent.
Fifth, on the scope of coverage of Bill C-24, it simply does not cover many of the major structural problems relating to Crown corporations. Bill C-24 is silent on matters of internal government organization; silent on the privileges and immunities of Crown corporations, for example, immunity from the Combine Investigation Act; silent on public servants on boards of Crown corporations; silent on the extent of the Government of Canada accounting entity; and silent on the creation of parliamentary oversight committees for Crown corporations. In addition, Bill C-24 covers only wholly-owned corporations. It does not apply to the more than 100 mixed and joint enterprises. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I make the point that the Bill is not at all in substance what it purports to be in form.

In other words, as my colleague has pointed out, the Bill is "a pig in a poke". It looks good to people who do not read it. The title is attractive. Some people have been fooled by it. However, the Bill, as I said at the beginning, really should be entitled "An Act to erode further Parliaments' existing very modest control over 183 federal Crown corporations and subsidiaries".

Mr. Speaker, may I thank you for recognizing me to speak on Bill C-24. Let me first state that the subject of Crown corporations and their control is not new to me. As a provincial minister for a number of years, I had the opportunity to create some Crown corporations. Perhaps the most noteworthy one was the Alberta Home Mortgage Corporation. I want to say that the administration, regulation and management of Crown corporations is not an easy or simple task. It is an awesome responsibility which is often thrust on ministers of the Crown who are simply not trained or equipped to handle the complexity of policy, direction or formulations within these complex conglomerates. In most cases it is not laws or even regulations which govern these giant public monopolies. It is essentially inertia, established practices, and most of the time a very powerful handful of very skilled top civil servants.
To my knowledge there now exist somewhere around 400 federal Crown corporations. The federal Government now taxes and recycles some 22 per cent of the entire Gross National Product of this nation. Much of this tax take is used up and recycled through public sector Crown corporations. All of these Crown corporations are supposedly responsible to Parliament for their financial administration, as well as their public relations and economic, social and structural accountability. Just how can Parliament, with some 282 Members, possibly keep a watchful eye on these 400 monolithic complexes? Unless some Members of Parliament, or even Senators, are placed in the front lines of policy and administrative decision-making in the Crown corporations, Parliament can only deal superficially with the results of maladministration, debilitative policy, innovation and choking inertia within the upper structural levels of these Crown corporations.
The only solution, Mr. Speaker, is to place elected Members or Senators from Parliament in the board rooms of these Crown corporations, so that they can report on and provide balance to the decision making at the very top. I have done this provincially and I can tell you it works. A new and needed dimension is added to the board room when one or more elected Members are present. Reporting to Parliament or even the Minister becomes instant rather than delayed. That is why I have on the Order Paper a Private Member's Bill to place elected House of Commons Members or Senators on the board of directors of federal Crown corporations. Senators could, and should, be used extensively as watchdogs in this regard. It would give a lot of them something to do. Surely if Senators are permitted to sit on the board of directors of private corporations, they should also have access to seats on the board of directors of federal public corporations.
The Hon. Minister, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), in his report New Legislative Proposals for the Control and Accountability of Crown Corporations, states that the Government will be responsible for the major strategic decisions of Crown corporations and must therefore be in a position to review their plans and requirements. Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend my allotted time on Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act dealing with Crown corporations, talking about one very important issue which my colleagues might find a little esoteric and somewhat arcane, but it is fundamental to our view of this legislation. It is important because it demonstrates a huge and gaping flaw in Bill C-24. It is also important because the Government has shown characteristic sloppiness in handling this issue, as the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) has repeatedly made clear.
The general issue relates to Clause 100 of Bill C-24, and in particular whether C-24 is binding on the Crown. As you know, Clause 100 restricts the incorporation or acquisition of new parent Crown corporations. If Bill C-24 is not binding on the Crown, as we on this side insist is the case, then Clause 100 leaves the Government with a huge loophole whereby it can continue to acquire or incorporate new Crown corporations with no scrutiny or control by Parliament.
Hon. Members will remember that that was the way the CDIC was acquired in 1982. Since then we have had the incredible problems with Canadair, de Havilland and the other Crown corporations. This is the way that Loto Canada was incorporated in 1975. The only time we hear of Loto Canada is
May 4, 1984

when it is in dispute with the provinces and the courts. This is the way that VIA Rail was acquired in 1978. Subsequently there have been shut-downs and changes in VIA Rail which drastically hurt western Canadians. There are other examples of this technique. It seems that the only time the Government is willing to go to Parliament on behalf of Crown corporations is for bail-out money, when it wants to write off $1 billion for Canadair or another $.5 billion for de Havilland, or throw away $125 million on Consolidated Computer Inc.
Section 16 of the Interpretation Act says, in effect, that a statute is binding on the Crown only if the statute expressly says it is binding on the Crown. This is very important when we consider the lessons of history. Hon. Members will recall that the Ontario and Supreme Courts recently held that the federal Combines Investigation Act did not bind the Crown in the form of Eldorado Nuclear Limited and Uranium Canada Incorporated in the so-called "Uranium Cartel" case, which is a national scandal. Why is this, Mr. Speaker? It is because the Combines Investigation Act does not say that it is binding on the Crown.
Our concern is that there is no clause in Bill C-24 which says that C-24 is binding on the Crown either. There was such a section, Clause 4, in Bill C-27 which was tabled by the Clark Government in 1979 relating to Crown corporations. There was a distinct move by the Clark administration to declare that these measures would be binding on the Crown.
What are the implications of this omission from this Bill? Simply put, Bill C-24, as now cast, does not remove the prerogative of the Crown to incorporate or acquire new Crown corporations by Order in Council as it has done in the past. Over the past decade this has been a means whereby the Government has intentionally and successfully evaded Parliament in the creation or acquisition of new Crown corporations.
How does this major loophole fit in with the Minister's statement that Bill C-24 would force all new Crown corporations to be created by, or pursuant to, an Act of Parliament? This is the claim which the Minister makes. However, it does not do that, Mr. Speaker. Was this an oversight? Was it a mistake? We think not. We think the "oversight" was intentional. We think the Government wants to keep this loophole. When this "oversight" was called to the attention of the Government, its response was "Oh, no, Bill C-24 is binding on the Crown. That was our intention". If it was the intention, Mr. Speaker, why does Bill C-24 not say so, as the Interpretation Act and the Supreme Court of Canada require?
Members opposite have told us that there are legal opinions that Bill C-24 is binding on the Crown. Where are these legal opinions? We have asked for them but have not seen one yet. Surely if there are legal opinions justifying the Government's actions, it should be prepared to table them. A senior Government official has stated that the head of the Department of Justice was of the view that Bill C-24 was binding on the Crown. Again, Mr. Speaker, we have asked for a copy or some verification of that opinion, but to no avail. Mr. Speaker, we do not believe that such an opinion exists. We do not believe that the Department of Justice feels that Bill C-24 is binding

on the Crown. We suspect that the Department of Justice has never held this view and that the Government ignored the advice of the Department of Justice and then had the dishonesty to suggest that the Department of Justice supported the Government's position.
Government Members wonder why Members on this side of the House do not trust the Government's word. We challenge the Minister and the Government right now. If there is a legal opinion from the Department of Justice, or from anywhere else for that matter, that Bill C-24 is binding on the Crown, table that opinion here and now. If the Government wants Bill C-24 to be binding on the Crown, as it says it does, then move an amendment right now to include the necessary clause in Bill C-24. To do otherwise leaves this Bill hopelessly flawed and grossly deficient and leaves the Government and the Minister open to a legitimate charge of callous and gross misrepresentation. To fail to bring in this amendment will allow this huge, gaping loophole to continue and will allow the proliferation of Crown corporations to continue.
Aside from my specific concern, I would like to discuss some of our basic concerns regarding this Bill. As the Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) has pointed out, it is basically a Bill which provides wide regulation-making powers rather than specifying details on control, direction and accountability. Without details, it is really impossible to know what the Government intends. For instance, some corporations are required to submit corporate plans, but the form and content of the plans are left to the regulations. This, of course, goes to the heart of our Party's position that Crown corporations should be accountable. Where there is a requirement for Crown corporations, and we agree that there is a requirement in some areas, they must be accountable to Parliament, and through Parliament to the public. These abusive powers and the secrecy which surrounds Crown corporations is a matter of direct concern to us.
Some of our specific concerns relate to the Minister's responsibility. This Bill leaves the Minister as de jure shareholder, but requires Cabinet to approve major initiatives such as appointments, approval of operating budgets and other details of running the Crown corporation. As my colleague from Capilano (Mr. Huntington) said, in being accountable to many, Crown corporations will continue to be accountable to no one.
Another of our specific concerns deals with directors. No details are provided on how the duties or responsibilities of directors will apply. More importantly, the Bill erodes the powers of a normal board of directors. In the private sector, the board usually monitors the performance of the chief executive officer. It sets the pay and can hire and fire based on performance. Under Bill C-24, this control is exercised by Cabinet. When one reviews the performance of Crown corporations and their boards of directors in the past, it is very clear how open to abuse and political patronage this system is. One need only think of the board of directors of Canadair to understand my point.

Financial Administration Act
Another of our concerns deals with the audit. This Bill gives considerable scope to the Auditor General. It does clarify the relationship between the Auditor General and the private sector auditors of Crown corporations. This has historically been a matter of concern for the Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), particularly in his role as Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee. However, we do not believe that the way in which this Bill deals with this issue is comprehensive.
I could deal, Mr. Speaker, with our concerns about the proliferation. As I have said, this Bill will continue to allow the Government to create new corporations by Order in Council. I could deal with the scope of the coverage. I could deal with many of our concerns about this Bill. However, you have indicated to me that my time has expired and I thank you.

Mr. Speaker, today we are debating once again Bill C-24, the Crown corporations Bill. The purpose of a second reading stage debate in our parliamentary lexicon is to determine whether or not the principles embodied in a Bill are worthy of the support of the people who represent the electors in this country in the Parliament of Canada.
Before any parliamentarian should support a piece of legislation, I believe he should have a sense of clarity in his mind as to whether there is a need for a particular piece of legislation. In that respect, I thought it might be instructive to review briefly for the House one particular Crown corporation which is close to the hearts and minds of those of us who live in the City of Calgary, Alberta. Of course, it is a fairly new Crown corporation which came into being mid-way through the 1970s. That Crown corporation is called Petro-Canada. It has had many subsidiaries that have grown like Topsy since it was initially formed.
Has that Crown corporation created a problem? I had never run for public office and was not a member of the Chamber when Petro-Canada was formed. I was merely a member of the community. I am sure Hon. Members will recognize that the oil and gas industry is important to the City of Calgary because it is a major employer and a prime source of economic health to that community. We have also discovered recently that it can be a major source of economic disaster.
Back in the 1970s Petro-Canada was established from funding by the Government of Canada through the Parliament of Canada. The first thing that corporation did was to hire employees from the marketplace. It was willing to pay 30 per cent to 40 per cent more than the marketplace was paying people at that time. This meant that it immediately distorted the marketplace and created, in effect, runaway inflation in salaries. In turn, this affected all of those companies that were previously in existence. The multinational and large corporations were able to compete because of the residual economic power they had, but it created enormous difficulties for small Canadian operators. That was the first effect of this Crown corporation.
Being a Crown corporation, it was subject to the laws of Parliament and the control of Cabinet. It operated in an industry that characteristically was mainly composed of what I would call peculiar people. I suggest that peculiar people are needed to meet the aspirations of such an industry. What we have in terms of the engineers and geologists who guide us in exploration work is a group of people who go to university for many years and obtain many years of experience, are willing to sit in the bush in temperatures of 30 and 40 degrees below zero for many days. They do this to help the country achieve self-sufficiency in oil and gas. I think that is peculiar. But those peculiar people are extremely skilled and very independent. They are special people in this country who are out in the field having to make life and death decisions instantly. They are responsible for millions of dollars of shareholders' money in the drilling of those wells. They have a particular temperament and philosophy and are willing to work 24 hours a day.
All of those are characteristics that do not hold well for employment by the Government in the bureaucracy. Nevertheless, the Liberal Government of the day decided to form that Crown corporation. It is now 1984. What do Calgarians see when they look at the Calgary skyline? They see the tallest building in town which has a red stone exterior. That tallest building is the PetroCan tower. It is a Crown corporation tower.
What does one find when one enters the front doors of that building? One finds that floor after floor of that immense tower are closed. One only sees emptiness because no one is working there.
Where did they get that stone?

Where did they get that stone, I am asked. It did not come from Canada. It was quarried in Norway, polished in Italy and placed on the exterior of a building in Calgary-primarily an empty building.
If one walks across the street into another building which has existed for some time, one sees that it is entirely empty. This building was leased by Petro-Canada and it is still paying rent for it today. There is no one in the building, yet the taxpayers of this country are paying for it every month, the result of a long-term lease.
Why did the Government of Canada buy service stations? Were those service stations in trouble? Was it a means of creating more employment? I do not think so.
The Government of Canada, through Petro-Canada, constructed a building which is now half empty. Furthermore, those employees who do occupy half of that building were transferred from buildings that are now empty and for which the Government is paying rent. As well, this is occurring in a city in which 25 per cent of the office space is vacant. Therefore one must ask why we have these two tallest buildings owned by the Government of Canada through its Crown corporation. I suggest that when one visits my City of Calgary to see this red building and walks through the front door, one is visually struck by waste.
May 4, 1984

Another example of waste by this Crown corporation concerns the long-term leases for drilling rigs which it entered into. Petro-Canada turned around and created another subsidiary Crown corporation to take those leases from the parent company since it could not use the rigs and had to pay for them. Petro-Canada now has a subsidiary Crown corporation that loses money while making Petro-Canada's bottom line look a little better.
In the five years that I have been here I have seen budgets introduced in this Chamber every year that have increased the cost for people to heat their homes and drive their cars. A tax has been placed on every gallon of gasoline and home heating oil solely for the purpose of enabling a Crown corporation to buy service stations.
Which they are now selling.

It now says that it will sell some of those service stations. At the same time, the Liberal Government during the last two years has voted to cut money that was allocated to senior citizens and money that was allocated for the purpose of education and health. Furthermore, the Government has introduced budgets that were designed to increase the amount of money that it could give to Crown corporations. It has traded pensions for senior citizens for extra cash to enable executives in Petro-Canada to fly first-class and to build half empty buildings.
There is a need for a Crown corporation Bill. It is sad that the Bill currently before this Chamber will do nothing to restore parliamentary accountability and control over those corporations.

Mr. Speaker, after looking at Bill C-24, I think the first two or three clauses alone would provide enough material for a speech of at least twenty minutes.
[English)
This Bill is supposed to cure a lot of things. However, what it has done is create greater confusion than hitherto. The first mistake was one of fundamental decision by the Cabinet, confusing the Financial Administration Act with the incorporation or the creation and control of Crown corporations. The two are disparate. The Financial Administration Act has existed since time immemorial. It has to do with certain practices of government. That is not the creation, maintenance
Financial Administration Act
and control of Crown corporations. The title is just a dog's breakfast-"An Act to provide for the Financial administration of the Government of Canada, the establishment and maintenance of the accounts of Canada and the control of Crown corporations". That is a total dog's breakfast. It is typical of this administration.
What do we do from here on in? Under Clause 3 we proceed to move by Order in Council. Orders in Council transferring the categories are tabled. They may be referred to a House committee for discussion and examination, and that is the end of it.
Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that after going to the trouble of referring an Order in Council made under Clause 3 of the Bill, under Subclause 2.2, an additional section thrown in there, the report which the committee may make cannot be debated. It states that within 15 days the Order in Council has to be tabled. Then it is referred to a committee. It states, and I quote:
(2) An order laid before a House of Parliament pursuant to subsection (1) stands referred, for a period of thirty sitting days commencing on the day on which the order is laid, to such committee of that House as may be designated or established by that House for the purpose.
If the Order in Council is referred to the committee and it produces a report on the Order, under Subclause (3) "no motion for concurrence in the report may be made in that House". What a gesture of fultility! The Order can be as false and full of trickery as that referred to by my colleague from Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski), SOR/84-350 dated May 1, 1984 dealing with lotteries and pools. That Order was made at eleven o'clock at night after getting the appropriate officials out and a quorum of three Ministers. That was to get away from the strictures of the Criminal Code. A fast shuffle of name was made. That should not be allowed.
We do refer Orders in Council to a joint committee of the House but that committee is very limited in its examination of such Orders in Council. It only examines whether there is power under the legislation to make an Order in Council, whether the Governor in Council subcommittee was properly constituted and that there is no retroactivity beyond that allowed in the legislation. That is all. Nothing can be said as to the content of the Order in Council, whether it is morally right, legally right or wrong.
The procedure that Australians follow is not open for us to follow. If we are speaking about Senate reform and the Senate serving a very useful purpose, we should speak about the Australian Senate. Orders in Council passed by the Government of Australia are submitted to the Senate for complete examination to determine whether those Orders in Council are within the power of the Government. Those things are done here in Canada. Further, however, the Australian Senate determines whether or not Orders in Council are right and whether or not they do an injustice to anyone. Frankly, if the

May 4, 1984
Financial Administration Act
Australian Senate does not like an Order in Council, it stands revoked. That is as it should be.
1 would say that within one year, Mr. Speaker, almost 50 per cent of government enactments could be passed by Order in Council. I came across an Order in Council the other day which was passed in 1981. This Order in Council affected the Immigration Appeal Board dealings with convention refugees. That Order in Council denied to Members of Parliament any access to written judgments unless the individual concerned or counsel for that individual had requested beforehand a written judgment with reasons. That is bureaucratic arrogance simply because Members of Parliament who inquire on behalf of constituents in immigration matters are acting as agents on behalf of those constituents just as much as any counsel acts as agent.
Bureaucrats who cannot stand outside examination of their actions deny Members of Parliament access to information by Orders in Council under some supposed right of privacy invented by the bureaucrats, interpreted by the bureaucrats and employed by the bureaucrats. The net result is that the ring of secrecy grows tighter all the time. Do not think, Mr. Speaker, that Members of Parliament can get that kind of information through the access to information legislation that has been passed. The people concerned only need say that, in their judgment, it would not be in the public interest to release the information that is sought. That is all there is to it.
1 would like to say right at the outset that the Bill is deficient, although many Members have shown it to be otherwise. For instance, certain schedules exist whereby Crown corporations may be moved from one column of a schedule to another column by Order in Council. There is no responsibility to Parliament. The Minister is the one to whom a Crown corporation shall be responsible.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would say that we should look at the proposal put forward by the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko). He proposes that our Government should emulate the governments of many European countries and of some provinces in Canada and place Members of the House or of the Senate on the boards of Crown corporations so that they can act as watchdogs as well as have access to specialized information regarding the operation of those Crown corporations. That would be a far superior addition to this Bill and would establish some form of control over these Crown corporations without having the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) and others be absolutely flummoxed by misleading reports from some Crown corporations which carry on business in some of Canada's major industries.
On that score, this is a bad Bill. This Bill should only serve as a white paper for reference to a committee so that that committee may see what can best be done with Crown corporations as we know them in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I would like to make some comments with regard to Bill C-24 which deals with the financial administration of Crown corporations. First I would like to talk about
some general aspects of Crown corporations per se and then I would like to look at some of the functions of Crown corporations. Third, I would like to underline some of the general failures of Crown corporations as we see them to be right now; and finally, I would like to offer some illustrations of some of the concerns expressed in my own riding regarding the operation of Crown corporations as they exist in Dauphin-Swan River.
First I want to say that Crown corporations in and of themselves need not be failures. Perhaps the Government has given Crown corporations a bad name because of its poor monitoring of Crown corporations. There has been a lack of accountability for Crown corporations at the creation stages, the developmental stages and any review stages further along the line. As has been outlined by a number of people today, what Crown corporations really need is a greater accountability to Parliament and a greater accountability to the public in general.
I do not think that anyone would quarrel with the fact that Crown corporations are a part of our national scene and, as the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) has stated, are a part of our entire economy. Crown corporations are viewed as being a part of our nation as a whole. I suppose it might be useful to contrast this situation with the one found in the United States simply to point out the uniqueness of Crown corporations in our national scene. Of the 100 largest corporations in Canada, ten are Crown corporations. Of the top 250 corporations in the United States, not one is a Crown corporation. Some of Canada's largest airlines, railways, radio and television networks and even one of the major oil companies are publicly owned, and of course, these companies have many subsidiaries as well.
Crown corporations cover a wide range of territory. In the area of transportation, there are Crown corporations such as the CNR, a company to which I will refer later in my comments. In the area of communications, there are Crown corporations such as the CBC and Canada Post. Later I wish to make some observations about the malfunctioning of Canada Post. In the area of energy there is Petro-Canada, and in the area of finance there is the Bank of Canada. Many people sometimes fail to realize that the Bank of Canada is in the same kettle of fish as the other Crown corporations because it has been perceived as an arm of government. Other Crown corporations in the financial area are the Federal Business Development Bank, the Farm Credit Corporation and Canada Mortgage and Housing. Of course, reference has already been made to Crown corporations in the industrial areas, such as Canadair and de Havilland. We find that Crown corporations exist in all areas of Canadian society.
It is important for us to recognize and underline the fact that it is not only the federal Government that is involved in Crown corporations but all governments, including provincial governments, regardless of political stripe, are involved. For instance, the Conservative Government of Ontario founded Ontario Hydro and the Saskatchewan Government is involved in the potash industry. As well, the Alberta Government has
May 4, 1984

shares in Pacific Western Airlines. All governments are involved in Crown corporations and they all face the same problem of accountability to which I referred at the outset of my speech.
It is not that governments do not know how to make Crown corporations more accountable but it is rather a problem of political will. Governments have not been willing to act in this area. However, as was mentioned by a previous speaker, there are some illustrations of the monitoring of Crown corporations at the provincial level. Whether we look at the British Columbia example or at the Saskatchewan example since 1946, we see that members of the Legislative Assemblies of those provinces have been involved in one way or another in monitoring or reviewing the work of Crown corporations. Some work has been done in that area.
I would like to underline at the outset that Crown corporations are a part of the national scene. Just because they have been given a bad name does not mean that they cannot be improved upon, but we would like to see a greater degree of accountability. I would like to suggest with regard to Crown corporations that even if we were to look at two functions which Crown corporations could serve, we would see that there is a place, if it is properly accountable, for Crown corporations to function in Canada, be it at the federal or provincial level. Of course, we do not usually refer to those agencies that are under the control of municipal governments as Crown corporations, but that is another area at which we could look.
Crown corporations could be vehicles of public policy. In other words, they could serve Canadians and fill the gaps within the system that a private enterprise may not meet. This has been recognized by some individuals. I would like to quote some remarks which were made by Pierre Franche, the President and Chief Executive Officer of VIA Rail. He said:
I believe Crown corporations often have a role to play where private enterprise does not want to play the role and the national interest demands it be played on private enterprise terms.
I have had conversations with the President, who was previously involved with the National Harbours Board, in trying to upgrade Churchill. Before he stepped into VIA Rail, I was pleased that he had a vision for VIA Rail. Unfortunately, at least in my riding, there has not been any kind of concrete evidence that his vision for areas that were served by VIA Rail is actually being realized. That is one of the functions which Crown corporations could serve.
The second type of function I would like to underline is the idea of providing some sort of economic direction, showing responsibility and generating some kind of economic climate wherein Crown corporations are working. There are different aspects which could be useful objectives for Crown corporations but, unfortunately, there has been a drastic failure in achieving the objectives generally, wherever we look. Public dissatisfaction with Crown corporations illustrates this on a national basis where the objectives or the functions are not
Financial Administration Act
being met. Enough has been said about Canadair and de Havilland that I do not have to emphasize this point.
Previous speakers have underlined some of the thorny problems which illustrate why the objectives have not been met on a national basis. A lot of this has occurred as a result of the lack of monitoring Crown corporations. The Government has allowed Crown corporations to stay away from many of their original functions. They have become autonomous entities unto themselves-going their own way, independent in their own actions without a'ccountability in any way, shape or form. It seems that a lot of board members and directors have lost their sense of accountability.
In conclusion, I would like to illustrate how Crown corporations have failed in specific areas, such as in my riding of Dauphin-Swan River. I could talk about the failure of the FCC, I could talk about the failure of the Federal Business Development Bank and others, but I would like to underline two failures in particular.
I would like to underline the failures of Canada Post and the failures of the Canadian National Railways. Canada Post, of course, has been one of the primary concerns for constituents in my area. I have received many many telephone calls, letters and petitions and I have had many conversations with regard to Canada Post's failure to provide service to the public, with regards to the withdrawal of service, and the negative impact that Canada Post has had on the local economy.
I see I am receiving a signal to conclude, Mr. Speaker. I would like to mention that the same thing has been true of the CNR. It has been making applications for the abandonment of rail lines, such as the one to Amaranth. In all of these, the Crown corporation has not acted in an accountable fashion. If there was more accountability, we might be able to make Crown corporations work in such a way that they would be of benefit to the people they are supposed to serve.
I appreciate the opportunity that I have had to share the concerns that we have in the riding of Dauphin-Swan River with regard to how Crown corporations are operating.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to make a few comments on Bill C-24 this afternoon. I would like to continue along the line on which my hon. friend from Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky) was speaking. He attempted to examine the function in our system of Crown corporations. He may have some doubt as to the function of Crown corporations and the system, although he should not have following his socialist philosophy, but there is no doubt that under the present circumstances the function of Crown corporations is to be the instrument of public policy. Whenever the Government wants to escape its responsibility and its accountability to the House of Commons and to the people it represents, it incorporates a Crown corporation and hides it away some place. So I have no problem understanding the function of Crown corporations. The problem is with the way that the system has grown like a cancer; it is totally out of control. The Government does not even know how many Crown corporations there are. The Canadian people do not

May 4, 1984
Financial Administration Act
know how many Crown corporations there are. They grow, are very dynamic and grow like a cancer.
I asked the Chairman of Petro-Canada in committee recently how many subsidiaries Petro-Canada had. He rattled off a few, but he was not sure as to the totality of the corporations in which it is involved, either wholly-owned or subsidiaries where it is a partner in joint ventures and so on. It is becoming a very dangerous situation. There is no way to make comparisons with any country in the western world in terms of their approach to this kind of exercise of government responsibility. There is no government responsibility, either in this Bill or in the existing structure. It is government irresponsibility.
My hon. friend from Dauphin says that the Government has given Crown corporations a bad name and that they do not have to be failures. I disagree with that statement. Crown corporations will always be failures because governments inherently-because it is the nature of the beast-cannot operate anything effectively and efficiently. It is against human nature to send bureaucrats and elected people out to run businesses. They are not good at it.
I would like to tell the House what Adam Smith said about corporate power. As we know, there are large corporations and so-called private corporations in Canada today that might as well be Crown corporations because they are so large, so cumbersome and so totally out of control that they not only influence public policy but dictate public policy. When they get into difficulty, of course, the first thing that they do is go to the bank and when the bank will not help them any more they come to the government and say "Bail us out". This happens all the time. There is no longer any accountability among big corporations.
Adam Smith told us 200 years ago, in speaking about corporate and public managers, that being the manager of other people's money rather than their own, it cannot be well respected that they should watch over it with the same anxious vigilance with which their partners in a private corporation watch over their own money. He said that negligence and profusion, therefore, must prevail more or less in the management of the affairs of a public company. That is what Adam Smith said 200 years ago and his words are just as relevant and true today. There is no way that an Ed Clark looking after a barrelful of money that does not have a bottom in it would be as vigilant and careful as someone else would be who was dealing with their own money. These corporate managers have their own language. It is an old subculture. It is the parallel structure of these people opposite who are completely out of control. They have their own language. Let me just quote-

Well, it is "inherently dynamic" because when we incorporated PetroCan, as you know, Sir, there were to be 180 or so employees in that particular company. It was to be a window on the world. It was to make deals with foreign lands-

It is out of control. You have no control over that place. Tell me how many subsidiaries PetroCan has, Mr. Deputy Prime Minister?

say?

Mir. Oberle: As many as it needs to exercise the Government's purpose, and the Government's purpose is to keep Canadians in the dark, to keep Parliament in the dark. Do not tell them anything. What about the executive officers of PetroCan, or any other Crown corporation? Are they elected by the directors? Oh, no, these are people appointed by these people opposite.

They make decisions over which Parliament and the Canadian public have absolutely no control. Let me ask the Acting Prime Minister another question. How many new jobs did PetroCan create last year? How many new barrels of oil has PetroCan found?

And show me in the PetroCan Bill where we gave it the authority to build service stations and get into the neighbourhood service station business. There is a legitimate role for government in the marketplace.

Just because the CNR, our great transportation system and our communication networks, have to become instruments of public policies because of the sheer geography and nature of our country, that does not mean we should get into the food chain business, that we should get into fertilizer, that we should get into selling gasoline in competition with private entrepreneurs.
Why not?
That is not being an instrument of public policy.
See if they can cut the mustard.
That is being greedy, centralist, socialist-
Hear, hear!
Well, you would like that, of course. These fellows over here are the socialists and, of course, they would like that; but they have nothing on these guys across the way.

They are so far ahead of you in their central planning, in their total integration and in their total concentration of all that has to do with the economy. You are babes in the woods. That is why you will be wiped out in the next election, because these people over there will be telling Canadians so many lies about the virtue of being in business and buying and controlling everything from Ottawa. They will be telling Canadians about all these virtues and, as the saying goes, some people can be fooled all of the time and some will be fooled once again.

They do not know how to run a Crown corporation. We know how.

But I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that you cannot fool all the people all the time and, therefore, there will be a change in government and we will have to rethink when that change comes how we want to build and rebuild our economic and corporate structure in this country.
Yea, Bennett!

Socialism, Sir, has been attempted for the last 15 years across the way. It has been attempted all over the world. These fellows are saying it does not necessarily have to fail, and it does not always necessarily have to fail; but it always does because socialism does not work except in heaven where you do not need it and in hell where you already have it.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be recognized for debate on Bill C-24. I thought you were going to recognize the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). I would be glad to defer to him. He seemed to want to get into the debate earlier.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have.

The Hon. Member indicates he has already spoken on the Bill, but I see he still has things to say. Perhaps he will get another opportunity.
There are many interesting features about this Bill and I want to go over a few of them in the few minutes which are available to me today. The first interesting feature is that the Opposition has been calling for some kind of reform in Crown corporation accountability for years, probably decades. So has the Public Accounts Committee. As the Speaker well knows, that is a relatively non-partisan but certainly all-Party Committee, and in many reports, which I will be referring to later, it has been calling for reform of Crown corporations. The Auditor General as well-and I will have more to say about him later-has been making a plea to the Government to improve the accountability of Crown corporations and others. The Government, for its part, has said that it also wants better accountability from Crown corporations and improved parliamentary control. Sadly, however, the result of its desire and deliberations is the Bill which we have before us today.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the Government, with all the power which is available to a majority Party running the Government, has produced a much watered down Bill-such a watered down Bill, in fact, that we in the Opposition who have been calling for reform have been forced to take a position opposed to a Bill which we had been calling for for all that length of time. That is also a very interesting feature of this Bill.
Third, the Government under the guise of consultation has politicized the office of the Auditor General by a ruse, I would say by a "rabbit out of the hat trick", if you like, and I refer to the well publicized letter of the Auditor General to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He also wrote one to the President of

May 4, 1984
Financial Administration Act
the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), who I see in the House today. In that letter to the Prime Minister, the Auditor General included this sentence-he was referring of course, to this Bill:
I am entirely supportive of this version of the proposed legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is a very exciting experience to speak in the House of Commons on a roaring Friday afternoon. It fills one with trepidation! I see my friend, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais), is present in the House this afternoon. I asked him to pay close attention to the speech I made earlier this week, which he did and for which I thank him.
Today I would recommend he pay attention to the business before him since I do not have much hope that the speech I am making will have any profound effect on changing the will of this Government, which seems hell bent on having this Bill proceed. The Government is forcing the Opposition to maintain its responsibility in opposing this Bill because we have to decide whether or not the principles of this Bill are worthy enough of support to allow it to go before committee. As so many of my colleagues have eloquently demonstrated, the principles of this Bill are not only insufficient but also defective. I compliment the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) for drawing our attention to the style, shall we say, exercised by the Government in eliciting the support of the Auditor General for this Bill. If that is an indication of support at a highly competent level, then this Bill is in pretty deep trouble.
I think it has been drawn to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that an analysis of Bill C-24 shows that there are several substantive reasons why we feel it should not proceed. The reasons we find it offensive are centered on the manner in which the Government will be permitted to make regulations concerning Crown corporations, the manner of their operations, the appointment of their boards and, particularly, the bypassing of the boards for the appointment of their chief executive officers. We feel that every section of substance in this Bill has attached to it a regulation-making power by the Governor in Council which is unspecified at the moment. Moreover, there is every reason to expect that the Government will change those regulations, having made them, without accountability to Parliament or without parliamentary input in those decisions. We feel, moreover, that there are no criteria established, especially for the manner in which corporations
Financial Administration Act
would be moved from schedule to schedule. That is the beginning of our analysis which has led us to oppose this Bill.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, the question of the rights of Parliament with respect to Crown corporations and the accountability functions of Members of Parliament. Apparently we have to make the point repeatedly that Parliament has no control over the creation of Crown corporations or of subsidiaries of Crown corporations. It is with regard to subsidiaries that the greatest proliferation is taking place. We have heard comments earlier today, as well as on other occasions, about the inability to count the total number of subsidiaries. I doubt whether we even have an accurate count of Crown corporations as such. The information on the number of subsidiaries of Petro-Canada, for instance, is simply not available. While Petro-Canada itself performs certain functions that are of benefit to the Canadian people, it is rather difficult to understand how it is of benefit to the Canadian economy for Petro-Canada to get into the service station business. Moreover, we think that there is insufficient accountability to the Government and Parliament about the way in which the subsidiaries of Crown corporations are run. As a result, the cost of the manner of operation is defective in that the controls are not strong enough.
Bill C-24 says that a Minister need not get parliamentary approval if there is in existence an Act giving the Minister power over a Department. We think the rights of Parliament are again bypassed in that way. When such matters are finally allowed to come before Parliament, the Bill stipulates that Members be confined to 30 days of debate in a committee and seven hours of debate in the House. This is entirely insufficient, particularly in the cases of major corporations which need reviews from time to time. I have already mentioned Petro-Canada. Air Canada is another corporation which surely needs close scrutiny by Members trying to exercise their responsibility to ensure that the best transportation system for Canadians is available at a time of great changes in deregulations in the industry generally.
I would like to discuss the matter of the composition of boards. The way in which this Bill would set up the membership of boards of directors would, in effect, turn them into advisory boards rather than actual boards taking the responsibility of decision-making. The Cabinet would appoint chief executive officers without any consultation with the board of directors of the Crown corporation concerned. If one considers the examples of Canadair and de Havilland, one must shudder at the prospect of the Government extending widely the principle of appointing senior management to Crown corporations without any reference at all to the boards of directors. I must ask what boards of directors are for.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few things about Bill C-24. I am sorry the previous Member did not have more time. I would like to extract a few points from the May 15 news release of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). There are a few interesting things in here that the Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and some other Tories seem to have overlooked.
The first thing is that the first Crown corporations in Canada were created in 1841. The first Canadian corporation in the form of a public enterprise was a Board of Work in the United Provinces of Canada created to construct a canal system in Canada. By the turn of the century, the Conservatives in this part of the country had taken on the development and management of Crown corporations on a large scale. Today, with eight Conservative provincial Governments, the Party Quebecois in Quebec, which is basically a Conservative Government, and the NDP Government of Manitoba, we find that the corporate holdings of the provincial Governments exceed those of the federal Government in terms of total assets represented. About 75 per cent of the provincial Crown corporations have been created since 1960.
We have an interesting situation here, Mr. Speaker. We hear Tory after Tory getting up and berating Crown corporations. They are not berating the theme of this legislation, the stated function of which is to bring more accountability for Crown corporations to Parliament and to Canada, which is a laudable intention. However, the Tories have not been pursuing that theme. They have been going after Crown corporations but have not bothered to point out the fact that their own Party at the provincial level is the greatest creator and developer of Crown corporations in Canada. They do not want to talk about Peter Lougheed's airline, PWA in Alberta or all the Crown corporations of Bill Davis, Grant Devine and so on. The litany of Crown corporations under Tory administrations goes on and on.
In almost every case, as the Deputy Prime Minister pointed out, there is far less accountability than is proposed in this legislation. However, the very nature of the Tory Party makes them play games in which they tell the electorate that they are opposed to Crown corporations and this kind of accountability for a variety of reasons, but they never bother to tell the truth
about Crown corporations and why they are created, which I believe is the responsible thing to do.
They have not pointed out why, as my colleague for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky) pointed out, ten of the largest corporations in Canada are Crown corporations while none of the 250 largest corporations in the United States are Crown corporations. We should reflect on that fact because of the nature of Canada and of our history with respect to the United States in particular which has tried to form a branch plant economy in Canada and has only allowed certain kinds of commodities to be created here while preventing us from using its technology and industrial resource base to expand into world markets. The United States has always held back and has returned the profits from Canadian labour, resources and capital back to the United States.
Crown corporations have been developed by socialist governments in Canada, Liberal governments and Tory governments. I should point out that this has been done to the greatest extent by Tory administrations. This is something that the Tories do not want to discuss because their corporate boardroom friends do not like it.
Let me address a number of shortcomings in this legislation which should be remedied. They are important questions to which a number of Members have spoken. There are various Crown corporations listed in the schedules of this legislation. For instance, there are 14 Crown corporations listed under Schedule B, such as the Atomic Energy Control Board, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission, national museums and so on. Schedule B at present includes 15 in the list, such as the Medical Research Council and the National Research Council of Canada. There are 29 listed under Schedule C, such as the Canada Ports Corporation, Loto Canada, The Royal Canadian Mint and so on. There are 26 listed under Schedule D, including Air Canada, Eldorado Nuclear, Petro-Canada, VIA Rail and so on. The list goes on.
Since I came here five years ago I have always been concerned about the fact that there is no one in Ottawa who can accurately say how many Crown corporations and subsidiaries exist. While the President of the Treasury Board has introduced a good measure, it should really alert Canadians to how insufficient accountability has been to this point. This has also been pointed out by Mr. Dye, the Auditor General. That provision appears at page 54 of the Bill at Clause 16. It states:
Each parent Crown corporation shall, within thirty days after the coming into force of this Act, send a copy of every by-law of the corporation in effect on the coming into force of this Act to the appropriate Minister and the President of the Treasury Board.
I submit that that is an open admission by the Government that it does not know what the bylaws are or what the Crown corporations are. This is a method of smoking them out.
The Government takes one further step with Clause 17, which states:
Notwithstanding section 100 of the said Act-

For the first time since Confederation, a piece of legislation has been introduced that will smoke out all of the subsidiary and parent Crown corporations so that they will come under one compilation, Schedule C, of this Bill C-24.
The simple admission by the Government that it is unaware of the bylaws of many of these Crown corporations and subsidiaries is alarming. However, it is beneficial to know that six months after the passage of this Bill all of those Crown corporations which have not filed with the Minister responsible as is required will cease to exist.
There are also some peculiarities written into this legislation which make it quite slippery, as is often the case with that side of the House. This Party has no representation in the Senate and does not intend to have any, particularly while that is a place where the democratic process does not occur.
