Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure today to be able to rise to discuss the Crown corporations Bill, Bill C-24. The mere necessity even to introduce the Bill to the House is an obvious admission on the part of the Government that the Government has totally lost control of Crown corporations. After listening to the previous speaker, and considering the support his Party has shown for the Government in the past few years, it is difficult to understand whether indeed they are for or against Crown corporations.
It is my intention this afternoon to demonstrate to the House the extent to which the control of Crown corporations has escaped the authority and influence of Parliament, which is where the control and influence over Crown corporations and their direction should be placed. In doing that, I will be dealing with the Canada Ports Corporation, which has particular significance in the areas of the Atlantic region and in the western region. I hope to be able to demonstrate through the use of the example of this corporation how out of control this whole matter of Crown corporations has become.
The Port of Saint John is one of the seven national ports of the country. It comes under the jurisdiction of the Canada Ports Corporation. The direction of the Canada Ports Corporation and of its predecessor over the last number of months has not been in the best interests of the port City of Saint John, nor of the people who live there. I would like to demonstrate why that is the case.
It will become obvious from the statistics and from the information which I am about to provide that the policies of the Canada Ports Corporation over the past number of years have had a detrimental effect upon the economic well-being of the Port of Saint John and upon the economic situation in that area. Because of the insensitivity of the Government, unfortunately the port has seen a steady decline in revenues, a steady decline in the amount of business channelled through it, and port activity has suffered considerably.
The first statistic with which I would like to deal concerns the commodity of flour. In 1980, 132,000 metric tons of flour was put through the Port of Saint John, whereas in 1983 it had declined to an amount of 63,000 mts. It is not that we have not addressed ourselves to this issue or that the House is unaware of the situation with reference to the shipment of flour and grain through the port. As a matter of fact, in June 1982, I brought to the attention of the Minister responsible for the

May 4, 1984
Financial Administration Act
Canadian Wheat Board the declining situation with reference to shipments of wheat. His response basically was that we should be satisfied with what we had been receiving and that the Government could probably justify itself by not even putting that number of shipments through the Port of Saint John. In terms of wood pulp in 1980, there were 5,506,000 mts put through that port, whereas in 1983 it declined to 368,000 mts. Lumber declined from 164,000 mts in the same year to 77,000 mts in 1983. On and on the story goes.
I understand that the recession has contributed substantially to the fact that revenues from port activities are down. However, 20 some years ago the Port of Saint John was a booming facility. It was one of the gateways of trade into Canada. Indeed, it was the bright spot for the future of that area. At that time, for reasons better known to the Government, it decided to open up the St. Lawrence River and sent up ice-breakers. That was the start of the process of decline in that region. There has been no greater threat to the economy of Saint John since that time. There have been several serious blows coupled with that situation since that time. For example, two major labour-intensive lines were lost to Saint John.
We require more positive action and a more positive attitude on the part of the Government. I am concerned because the Bill does not address itself to the situation. I am glad to see the former Minister of Transport sitting here this afternoon. I hope he will take to heart some of the very serious matters which I am bringing to his attention and will pass on the information to his colleagues. Perhaps we will see some positive results.
If we are to keep pace with the competition, if we are to deal with dwindling cargoes and things of that nature, there must be a positive attitude on the part of the Government. That has not developed over the past, despite the fact that this port is one of the most efficient in Canada. Its labour productivity is second to none. If the figures on the tonnage handled per man-hour are examined, it becomes obvious that the Port of Saint John is the most productive in the country, including those of Montreal, Quebec and other regions. It is incumbent upon the Government to recognize the efficiency and the difficulties which that port is presently experiencing. It employs 6 per cent of the labour force in that part of the country, yet the Government continues to ignore that fact or that it utilizes 5.8 per cent of disposable income in that area. It is the economic heart of Saint John. The port is an extremely valuable facility. Business and labour have indicated their willingness to co-operate with the port. In fact, the port has demonstrated its goodwill in its labour contracts and in its ability to get along. We now need co-operation and sensitivity from a government which has been unwilling to demonstrate this in the past.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate this afternoon in this extended debate on Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation
to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof.
It is interesting to note that while it has taken the Government over four years to come to grips with the issue of Crown corporations, even in its inefficient and inadequate manner, the previous Government, under the leadership of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), managed to come to grips with the entire issue in a matter of about six months. In its short term of office, it was able to present a Bill which would have dealt with the entire problem of Crown corporations.
I am not inclined to argue with my colleague who preceded me, but he suggested that Crown corporations were out of hand. I think I know what he meant; in a sense he was right. However, Crown corporations as far as the Government is concerned are very well in hand. They are just exactly the way the Government wants them so that it can carry out, through the mechanism of Crown corporations, the kinds of activities it wants to do in secret. The Government wants to keep these activities secret from the House of Commons and from the people of Canada. We can find example after example of exorbitant amounts of money being spent by the Government to bail out Crown corporations such as Canadair.
There is no doubt in my mind that the Government has been deliberately slow in bringing in any reforms in the whole arena of Crown corporations. It knows perfectly well that the needed reforms will not be the ones which will suit it in terms of allowing the Government to exercise the devious sort of control it would like to have over a large sector of the Canadian economy.
The Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) and the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) have spent a lot of time studying this Bill. They have spent much more time than many of us have and certainly have identified many of its weaknesses. In fact, when one first looks at the Bill, one would be inclined to think that it was attempting to address some of the real problems existing in Crown corporations.
In listening for a short time this afternoon and this morning to my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) and Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), we are convinced that there is a superficiality to this Bill. It does seem to address the issues of Crown corporations which have been of concern to Members of Parliament. However, when you read the Bill carefully, you find it has not achieved that. The one problem with Crown corporations, the failure to be accountable to Members of Parliament in particular, is not dealt with in this Bill.
I want to deal with the problems and issues raised by this Bill which have not been addressed adequately. As I mentioned, accountability is the predominant problem. The concept of Crown corporations is not new. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) gave the Conservative Party credit for a lot of the past history of Crown corporations. He is quite right that we have been involved and supportive over the years.
May 4, 1984

Contrary to what he says, we are not critical of Crown corporations per se. We feel there is a real need for Crown corporations.
Get your act together.

Our act is together. We all agree there is a need for Crown corporations in certain circumstances. The difference is that we want Crown corporations to be accountable to this House of Commons and the people of Canada, not accountable to the Cabinet, which has been the experience with this Government. That is why it does not want to see any major changes. It knows that a worthwhile change would take away the privilege of the Government to make changes by Order in Council when making appointments and paying debts of Crown corporations in difficulty without any recourse or consultation with Parliament.
One of the most interesting writings on Crown corporations was contained in a presentation given at a conference on Crown corporations in Toronto last fall. The presentation was made by Professor Robert Prichard, a visiting professor of law from Harvard Law School. The presentation was entitled Reforming Crown corporations. He looked at the whole subject in a very thorough manner and tried to make a diagnosis of the problems. He boiled that down to seven major problems and concluded the presentation by what he called "the treatment".
Let me dwell on his seven-point diagnosis. First, the problem is aggravated and compounded by the fact that Crown corporations have proliferated at a rapid pace over the last number of years. As my colleague said, if you ask an official of the Government or a member of the Cabinet how many Crown corporations we have, it is almost impossible to say on any given day how many there are in existence. This proliferation compounds the problem of trying to cope with them.
Second, it is evident that there has not been established an adequate legal and jurisdictional regime to deal with the accountability problem of Crown corporations. This is something we in the Official Opposition would like to see. This is one of the main problems with Crown corporations.
The third item identified in the diagnosis is what he termed the bureaucratization of the accountability process. Bill C-24 just aggravates that situation. We find in this Bill that Crown corporations may be responsible to Cabinet and have certain responsibility to individuals, but there is no consistency in dealing with the problem of where the accountability lies with Crown corporations. There is a mishmash of responsibility, which leads to a definite undermining of the whole process of accountability.
The fourth item has to do with the resistance among bureaucrats to changes in the accountability process. That naturally does not fit in with the concept of the bureaucrats to increase their power and dominion. They object to anything in a Bill such as Bill C-24 that would lessen their opportunity to exert influence at this level.

The fifth item is something we cannot get away from, that is, the politicization of appointments to boards. I have had a little experience in getting to know individuals who are on boards. During the last year it has been my pleasure to know three people who were appointed to a recently-created Crown corporation. One is a chief executive officer. These people perform impeccably well in the private sector. I do not look upon them as being strongly politicized individuals. They may have some leanings, I do not know, but they were successful in their individual enterprises. I hope they will not be disappointed when they take on their role on the board of directors. They may find that the role they played in the private sector is not open to them in the same manner.
I find that there is not enough time left for me to discuss the treatment. I appreciate the opportunity of presenting the problem that exists with Crown corporations.

Mr. Speaker, it is time that we had an opportunity to examine, even in a superficial way, the proliferation of Crown corporations in this country and the aberration caused in the business community with regard to Canada's economic demise as a competent nation. It evolves around all that we are looking at today with regard to the chaos which has resulted for many businessmen and individuals. There is a horrendous list of bankruptcies. This has produced an almost static figure of 1.5 million unemployed. This has been the case for month after month and there is little possibility that these people will soon get back into the work force.
An examination should be made of the proliferation of these Crown corporations. If you go back to 1962, you will find that a totally new socialistic approach developed with regard to the role of the private sector as compared to the public or government sector.
We have gone from something like 28 Crown corporations to Lord knows how many. You can start around 300 and work up to 600 and find some justification for saying that they have the mark of a Crown corporation. Today there are almost as many individuals working for Crown corporations as there are working in the Public Service of Canada. I believe there are over a quarter million people employed in the various Crown corporations. Another type of partial employment is available through the directorships of these Crown corporations. While there may be examples of very worth-while people who are making a contribution in one way or another to these Crown corporations, boards of directors of Crown corporations have become the Liberal Party's greatest porkbarrel in the history of the nation.
During this debate, many of my colleagues have asked what is the role of a director of a Crown corporation. Becoming a director of a given company in the private sector is dependent upon a personal track record of achievement in whatever sector of the economy one has developed an expertise. Everyone who is appointed as a director of a significant private-sector company in the country has a proven success record.

Who ends up paying those bills, Mr. Speaker? We do.
I happened to take a look at the April 30, 1984, issue of Fortune magazine. A statement on politics and policy in that magazine contains a discussion of the Mitterrand Government in France and its socialistic tendencies which have got France and the French people into difficulty. When looking at some of the comparisons used in that article regarding the difficulties of given nations with their external debts-I see that as an example-Canada's external debt exceeds those of Mexico and Brazil, two countries which we call almost bankrupt. Canada's debt exceeds Argentina's debt as well. As a matter of fact, according to these figures, Canada's external debt is $99.5 billion or 34 per cent of the gross domestic product, whereas Argentina's external debt is $36.5 billion and represents 30 per cent of its gross domestic product. It is not very pleasant to pick up an article like this and see what our financial rating is in comparison with that of other countries in the world, especially when those other countries are in real economic difficulty.
The Government of Canada tries to make us believe that everything is great and wonderful. It tries to make us believe that tomorrow will be a wonderful day, except for the fact that no one seems to have any respect for our dollar. Our dollar is costing the taxpayers of the country high interest rates, a lack of jobs and a lack of housing starts. Who is going to start to build a house now while watching us go down the road again to the high interest situation that destroyed many Canadian families not more than a year and a half ago? Yet billions of dollars are now being spent in an attempt to prop up a dollar that was a disgrace to start with and is worth 77 cents U.S.
Therefore, I would say that we do not need a Bill that is as anaemic as is this Bill. It is anaemic in comparison with our hopes for ever having control over the proliferation of Crown corporations, the incompetence of Crown corporations or the destructiveness to the private sector of Crown corporations. What we in Canada need is the elimination of incompetence and the elimination of many of the Crown corporations that go along with it. We certainly need some form of protection to
eliminate the porkbarreling that goes on with the appointments of Grits only to the directorships of these boards. These Grits receive free plane tickets and free directors' fees for doing next to nothing. They end up finding out that for all of their incompetence, they are paid huge bonuses. That is the situation with de Havilland and that is the mess in which we find ourselves. The only way we are going to get out of that mess is by getting rid of these people and putting in power some people who will put some sense into the economy of the country.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps this Bill was introduced at this time in an attempt to appease the public and the parliamentary outcry over scandals like Canadair. If that is so, it is quite clear that its purpose was not to place Crown corporations under effective public control but to appear to place Crown corporations under effective public control. There is an old saying that British justice must not only be done but must be seen to be done. It appears that this Government does not believe that justice needs to be done but that only the facade need be created.
Previous speakers have pointed out many of the flaws in the Bill. There is no control over subsidiaries. The parent company may escape all of its real obligations by simply emptying itself into those subsidiaries that have already been pioneered. There is no control of the regulations. There is no assurance that elected representatives will be able to receive all the relevant facts, and there is no opportunity for elected representatives to debate certain reports and reject them if they find them to be faulty. This is not too surprising because, contrary to the statement of the badly informed Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), Crown corporations are not a socialist invention. If, as he said, they only work in hell, it is because they were invented by capitalist governments.
At times, the CCF and NDP have used something like a Crown corporation as a model, because it was the only thing available under the current federal structure and laws of the country. However, for a century and more back, Crown corporations typically have been created to meet the needs of the most pressing and aggressive business people in the private business world. Until the late 1930s, that was generally done under the leadership of federal Tory Governments, and since then it has been done under the leadership of federal Liberal Governments.
The Tories, of course, feel that they have been shut out from what they call the porkbarrel and they want in again. In the meantime, as was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), they are doing quite well with their provincial porkbarrels. Crown corporations were not created to serve the common people. They were created to serve the needs of big business. One need only look at Ontario Hydro to see a clear example of that at the provincial level.
I would first like to mention some examples of that which I have just indicated. Canadian Pacific created the means for investors to open up the West, to get at the minerals and other raw materials of the country, and to make a bundle by shipping farmers to the West.

Of course, Canadian Pacific is the most famous example of a corporation cheating taxpayers by taking subsidies given by taxpayers, and then reneging on commitments to provide transportation either for passengers or for freight. Its successor, VIA Rail, which was really created as a smokescreen for the CP, or the CP-CN, has established an amazing record of being totally free from the control of Parliament. During 1981 and 1982, Opposition Parties tried in every way to get some control over VIA Rail's cutback of 20 per cent of its service. The Government simply laughed at us and protected VIA Rail.
Canada Post has become a Crown corporation. Its prime function now is not to serve the individual person who writes letters, but to serve commercial corporations. It is cutting back on the service to individual letter writers and letter receivers.
There is also the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which for four decades has been following the purpose of funding private investors who are rent-gougers in the real estate industry. There is a small veneer of non-profit subsidy, but most of the subsidy goes to unlimited rental units and rent-gougers. They are now getting into the business of rent supplements, whereby the public purse will simply be used as a way of funnelling money to an unlimited degree to the private profit corporations which are monopolizing the apartment industry in the major cities of Canada.
In reference to housing, there is an example, not of a Crown corporation but of a public corporation that I think ought to be given more consideration in addressing this Bill on the question of the control of Crown corporations. The City of Toronto created a non-profit housing corporation. It did that for the same reason as that for which Crown corporations have been created, it being mainly that a certain major public need was not being met by private industry. The City of Toronto Non-Profit Housing Corporation has many problems. It started out with a great lack of experience and had to learn through a good many of its mistakes. One of its major problems was the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-the delays, misleading statements, reneging on promises, changing of rules in midstream and then the use of changed rules in order to milk not only non-profit corporations but co-ops by changing the basic rent rules after the general program had started. Nevertheless, the City of Toronto Non-Profit Housing Corporation has created low to moderately-priced housing for thousands of people in the City of Toronto who otherwise would not have been able to get it. These people would have had extreme difficulties in finding decent housing. What the City of Toronto Non-Profit Housing Corporation has that does not characterize the Crown corporations that the Government proposes to set up is, first of all, that city council has access to
Financial Administration Act
all the facts. It has a mixed board, made up of members of council and other citizens. We can argue about the proportions, but the fact is that council members have direct access to all the facts. The board is annually appointed, which means that the whole council can carry out an annual review. As well, the tenants have a right to appear before the board of directors to state their case. The tenants and the public can obtain information so that at the next general election of the members of the council they can, if they wish, elect councillors who will renovate, improve or correct the Toronto Non-Profit Housing Corporation.
That sort of strength, health and accountability is in no way provided by this Bill. What is really needed federally is legislation which would do the equivalent of what has been done municipally in Toronto and in other places. For one thing, we must remove the immunity of the Crown from ordinary scrutiny and litigation. Consider the scandal of a Crown corporation such as Eldorado being used to protect a whole group of private entrepreneurs who had engaged in a cartel by claiming that because of its being a Crown corporation the matter could not be brought before the courts. That protection must be removed from any Crown corporation legislation.
There must be provision for representation by workers at all levels in the industry. There must also be provision for representation by the users, because it is they who are the watch-dogs, not Parliament. Parliament can be useful in a limited way, but without the people who have the direct experience as workers and as users of the activity of the Crown corporation, Parliament can never be well enough informed to do its job. Above all, there must be guaranteed public access to all the facts, not only by some limited Senate committee or some limited parliamentary committee. There is no good reason why the basic facts of past operations of a publicly-owned corporation need be kept secret. There could be the usual discretionary secrecy when engaging in real estate buying or personnel decisions, which are taken by the City of Toronto Non-Profit Housing Corporation, but the books of the past are open and should be so.
I think the Government should junk this Bill, and bring in a Bill that really meets the need of the public, the need for public corporations that could be controlled through public representatives.

subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME
PROPOSED EXTENSION OF DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should, at the next Federal-Provincial Conference, consider the question of extending daylight savings time an additional two months.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion reads that, in the opinion of this House, the Government should at the next federal-provincial conference consider the question of extending daylight savings time an additional two months. It should be noted that although local time falls under provincial or municipal jurisdiction, official time is the responsibility of the federal Government.
The National Research Council presented a publication in 1983 recommending that daylight savings time be introduced on March 1, two months earlier than at present. The report states that recent interest in energy conservation has led to detailed studies of the possible advantages of longer periods of daylight savings time. It appears that significant savings in energy would result if daylight savings time were to start nearer the beginning of March and end about a week later in early November. The main energy saving is attributable to reduced consumption of electricity for evening residential lighting.
Year round daylight saving was first used in some countries during the Second World War. It was used in both Quebec and Ontario from September 1940 to September 1945, and throughout Canada from February 1942 until the latter date,
May 4, 1984

by federal Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act.
In summary, it can be stated that while the use of daylight savings time is of questionable value in rural areas, in the westernmost portions of certain time zones and in the most northerly areas, it is well accepted by most people in Canada and the United States. It is probably only a matter of time before a move to an extended period is made in both these countries.
The National Research Council has been on record as supporting the extension of daylight savings time since 1974 when the United States experimented with daylight time the year round. Mr. C. C. Costain, head of the Council's electrical and time standards section, has stated that much better than year round daylight savings time would be a symmetrical system with about four months of daylight time after July 1 as is the case currently, and four months instead of two months before July 1. During March and April there would be enough light for schoolbound children in the morning and an extra hour for everyone in the afternoon. The Council would also like to see a one-week extension of daylight time in the fall so as to ensure plenty of light in the early evening on Hallowe'en, October 31.
The National Research Council stated that $23.8 million a year could be saved in the reduced use of electricity, the number of traffic accidents would decrease, the crime rate would drop, the economy would be sparked by increasing retail store business and school children would return home in daylight. The Province of Saskatchewan is on extended daylight savings. There would also be psychological benefits during winter blahs.
Currently before the United States Senate, a Bill is being debated which would advance daylight savings time by two months. A decision is to be reached later this year and should the Bill pass, it is expected that Canada will follow by adopting the same plan.
In the summer of 1983 I questioned my constituents of Winnipeg-Assiniboine regarding their feelings on the issue of extending daylight savings. Some 83 per cent favoured an extension, while some wished to have daylight savings time year round, similar to Saskatchewan. Only 12 per cent were against it and 5 per cent were undecided. As there was such an overwhelming majority of constituents who supported this proposal, I contacted the Hon. James Lee, Premier of Prince Edward Island, who is to be the next chairman of the annual premiers conference, and asked that he place the subject of extending daylight savings time on the agenda of the conference. In response to my letter, Premier Lee stated:
My colleagues and I in the Council of Maritime Premiers support the extension of daylight savings time and indicated this in a press release in September, 1982.
The next annual Premiers' conference may be an appropriate forum in which to raise this subject for discussion by the ten Premiers.
The press release which Premier Lee refers to in his letter read as follows:
Daylight Savings Time
The Council of Maritime Premiers said that if the United States Senate approved a bill now before it to begin daylight savings time on the first Monday of March each year, about eight weeks earlier than is now the case, the three Maritime Provinces would urge similar action be taken in Canada.
The U.S. proposal, which has already received approval from the House of Representatives would result in energy savings. Should this become a possibility, it must be implemented in as many areas of North America as possible because of the integrated transportation and communication systems on this continent.
I also received a letter of support from Premier William Davis of Ontario who stated that:
Ontario would be more than willing to consider supporting the extension of daylight savings time if it is also supported and adopted by the other Provinces and by the United States.
As well, there are many other advantages to extended daylight savings time. For example, it has been noted that golfers could leave work at five o'clock and still get 18 holes in before the sun goes down. There are also many housewives who like to golf in the evening as well, so they would be able to go along with their husbands. Of course, this would be more of a benefit to golfers in the United States because our Canadian climate effectively limits our golf season.
If, as in Saskatchewan, it was determined that Canada should be on daylight savings time year round, Air Canada would not have to spend so much money and time on updating flight schedules. The United States is intent on adding a bit of sunlight to the afternoon. As a matter of fact, if legislation does not get the sunlight, technology will. Two NASA scientists postulate that 16 collapsible mirrors could be placed in low earth orbit and then propelled into an orbit 22,500 miles above the continental U.S. At that height the mirrors could track the earth's rotation and, directed by computers, could slowly direct a beam of sunlight from city to city, adding a few hours to the length of each day. It is estimated that this would save the equivalent of $285 million in energy every year and pay for itself within five years. I believe, however, that extending daylight savings time through legislation would be much easier.
I am suggesting that the subject of extending daylight savings time be discussed at the next federal-provincial conference. The ten Premiers could then consider the pros and cons of implementing this proposal in their respective provinces. There has been no response or comment from the west in this regard, and the western Premiers could request that their citizens let their feelings be known on the extension of daylight savings time.
